case_title: Markash Jajara v. State of Assam & Anr.
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor (described as having poor financial conditions)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (son-in-law; husband of the accused's daughter)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (Exception I of s.300 IPC considered by the Supreme Court)
evidence_type: Extra-judicial confession (oral, to daughter and villagers); testimony of victim's wife (PW-6) on confession and victim's conduct; medical evidence (post-mortem and autopsy surgeon); circumstantial evidence (incident inside accused's house, accused alone with body); non-eyewitness testimony of victim's brother (PW-8)
confession: Extra-judicial oral confession by the accused to his daughter (PW-6) that he murdered the victim with a bamboo stick, also reported by PW-1 (confession before villagers). Courts below relied on it heavily; the Supreme Court read PW-6's evidence in its entirety and accepted that the accused caused the injuries.
aggravating_circumstances: Fatal head injury (three lacerations on head, per post-mortem and autopsy surgeon); no other aggravating facts noted by the Court
mitigating_circumstances: Grave and sustained provocation by the victim's drinking and ill-treatment of the accused's daughter; loss of self-control; no premeditation; motive to protect daughter rather than to kill; accused's poor financial condition
trial_court_outcome: Guilty under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000 (six months simple imprisonment in default)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (conviction under s.302 IPC replaced by culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
neutral_facts: The victim, who had been living with his in-laws for about three to four months, was found dead inside the house of the accused by the victim's brother, who had gone there after learning that the victim had been assaulted. The brother lodged a first information report the same day stating that the accused had struck the victim with a bamboo stick. The body was lying on the kitchen floor. The post-mortem report recorded three lacerations on the victim's head, and the autopsy surgeon opined that the head injury was fatal and caused instantaneous death. The brother was not an eyewitness. The victim's wife, the accused's daughter, stated that she was away at work and returned around 4 p.m. to learn of the killing; out of fear she did not enter the house until police arrived. She stated that she questioned the accused, who confessed to having murdered the victim with a piece of bamboo. She testified that the victim was an alcoholic who quarrelled with her and the accused after drinking and ill-treated her. The accused's wife supported the prosecution to the extent that the victim was killed by the accused, but did not witness the occurrence. A witness stated that the accused confessed before villagers. The accused was arrested and a chargesheet was filed. The prosecution case rests on the confession, the fact that the incident occurred inside the accused's house, and the accused being alone with the body.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from three head lacerations (forehead, left mastoid region, below chin); autopsy surgeon opined the head injury was fatal and caused instantaneous death
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 finally upheld (s.302 conviction modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation or planning
motive: Accepted by the Court: to prevent the victim from misbehaving with the accused's daughter after consuming alcohol, and to force him to mend his drinking and ways
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-6 read in entirety, including cross-examination on victim's alcoholism and ill-treatment; statement that the accused and victim were the only ones present in the house; post-mortem findings and autopsy surgeon's opinion
witness_credibility: Supreme Court found PW-6's version, including her admissions on the victim's conduct, deserved appreciation in its right perspective; PW-8 admittedly not an eyewitness
post_offence_conduct: Accused confessed to daughter when she questioned him about the incident; was taken to the police station after police arrived
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: 03.10.2016; High Court: 12.03.2019; Supreme Court: 03 November 2023
legal_representation: Appellant: Gaurav Agrawal, Advocate. State of Assam (respondent): Nalin Kohli, Senior AAG, with Aastik Dhingra, Anshul Malik and Shuvodeep Roy, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR registered under s.302 IPC on ejahar of PW-8; accused arrested; chargesheet filed; nine prosecution witnesses examined; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: guilty under s.302, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; culpable homicide not amounting to murder; sentence reduced to ten years rigorous imprisonment
defence_argument: Not stated in Supreme Court proceedings; before the High Court the defence argued there was no eyewitness and that the alleged confession to the daughter could not be relied upon
legal_principle_applied: Exception I to s.300 IPC (grave and sudden provocation; sustained provocation considered; provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked)
precedent_relied_upon: None cited by the Supreme Court; High Court relied on Ajay Singh v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 12 SCC 341 on the wording of extra-judicial confession
sentencing_rationale: Ends of justice adequately met by reducing life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment of ten years, given the provocation and absence of premeditation
judicial_mitigating_factors: Persistent and sustained provocation by the victim's alcoholism and harassment of the accused's daughter; loss of self-control; no pre-meditated intention; motive to protect daughter
other_sentence_order: Release on completion of reduced sentence unless required in any other case; pending interlocutory applications disposed of
